title: Is the complete-pivoting growth factor exactly 8 for 8x8 matrices?
credit: A. Edelman & J. Urschel 2023, arXiv:2303.04892 (also Cryer 1968, Gould 1991 for the g_n <= n history)
premise_risks: Exact values g_n are known only for n ≤ 4 (Cryer; Cohen: g_3 = 2.25, g_4 = 4). g_5 = 4.1325 is only conjectured (proved g_5 ≤ 4.84, Edelman–Urschel arXiv:2602.20390, preprint) and g_6 ≥ 5 is only a lower bound. Determining g_7 is therefore much harder than an n ≤ 6 baseline suggests.
plain: The worst-case complete-pivoting growth is known exactly only for n ≤ 4 (values 1, 2, 2.25, 4). For n = 5 the best known value 4.1325 is only conjectured optimal, with proved upper bound 4.84 (Edelman–Urschel, arXiv:2602.20390), and for n = 6 the value 5 is only a lower bound. The value g_8 = 8, attained by Hadamard matrices, is conjectured but unproven, and Hadamard matrices are known not to be optimal at n = 12 and 16. Determine g_7 and decide whether g_8 = 8.
math: With $g_n$ as above (real matrices, complete pivoting), prove or disprove $g_8=8$ (equivalently $g_8\le 8$, since an $8\times8$ Hadamard matrix has growth exactly $8$). Determining $g_7$ (known lower bounds from Edelman–Urschel Table 1) is a separate question, not part of the claim. Background: $g_n$ is known exactly only for $n\le4$; $g_5\le4.84$ (arXiv:2602.20390).
